YANKS IN THE ST.MIEHL SALIENT.

A remarkable photograph of streams of American soldiers pouring into the St.Mihiel salight,with continuous pressure on the retreating enemy. In the background may be seen the famous Mount.Sec,strongly fortified by the Germans but captured by the Americans in the course of the first day of the assault. The soldiers in the foreground are machine-gunners;their column is crossing the route of a supply train.

AMERICAN MARINES AND NEWMODEL ANTI-AIRCRAFT MACHINE GUN
MARRIS AIR UNSAFE FOR GERMAN FILTERS.

The German Taubs and other air machines serve as targets when the American Marines are on the job in France. These soldiers of the Sea Are a part of the American Expeditionary Forces and are ready to train this modern weapon on any German plans that might come within range. This anti-aircraft machine gun is a new model. RELEASED MARCH 18th,1918.

Americans in Alsace picking off Boches with a 37mm gun on the parapet of a second line trench. These guns are known among the Yankee Infantrymen as the "trouble makers" - both because the one-pounders do considerable damage to the enemy and because the enemy nearly always makes things as warm as possible in the neighborhood where a one pounder is set up.

BABY TANKS PROVE EFFECTIVE IN ALLOWED ADVANCE.

The worth of the small tank was thoroughly demonstrated during the recent Allied advance. The effectiveness with which these "babics" smashed the Hirndenburg line has renored them absolutely indispensable to an infantry advance. The photo is one of the first received of an American tank crew in France. They are shown priming the motor for preparedness is the watchword with all Americans.

FIRST PHOTO OF AMERICAN IN THE FRONT LINE TRENCHES: - HALTING THE HUN AT THE LORRAINE GATE.

No training trenches are these, but the grim reality. Here is the first picture of our boys at the actual fighting front holding a portion of the Lorraing sector against the Teuton horses whose tide of invasion has been stemmed. Here are your sons fully equipped and fighting your battles. No words can express the sadness with which these men took up their active participation in this world wide war, for now at last they are as one with the Allies fighting the battles of and for the world.

FUNERAL OF FIRST AMERICANS TO DIE IN FRANCE.

Impressive rituals marked the burial of Corporate James D.Gresham, Private Thomas F. Enright and Private Private Merle D.Hay, of Company F. 16th Infantry, who were interred with religious and military ceremonies at Bethelmont on the afternoon of November 4th. Throughout the ceremony at the graves, French batteries, from their positions, fixed minute guns over the village at the German trenches. General Bordeaux, who officiated at the services in the name of the French Army, "bid farewell to all that was mortal of the three heroes." 3/2/18

WHO'S HAPPIEST ON ARRIVAL OF OUR TROOPS IN FRANCE THAT COUNTRY OR OUR BOYS?

It is a great question which is more pleased upon the arrival of our troops in France, that country or our troops themselves. To our boys in olive drag it meant that the hardest part of an arduous training period was over, and that they soon would get an opportunity to show the world their fighting qualities. Though the arrival of the boys in France was unheralded, the first strains of "Dixie" brought the enthusiastic population out of their homes in one clamorous welcome.
